chunks.title: Workbench — Overview
chunks.text:
Workbench (#/workbench). Overview.
Description:
Workbench is a multi-track video editor for the things you generate in SmartVideo. You drop your generated videos, images and audio onto a timeline, add motion cards, sound and themes, edit with an AI chat, and export an MP4 from your browser.
Summary:
Edit your generations with motion cards, sound and AI chat on a multi-track timeline.
About:

chunks.title: Workbench — Overview
chunks.text:
Workbench (the Motion Workbench) is a post-production editor shown inside SmartVideo. It has a library on the left (Media, Motion, Sound and Themes tabs), a live preview in the middle, a Properties inspector on the right and a multi-track timeline at the bottom. You bring in your own generations (images, videos and audio made in other studios) with the + Add your generations button or the Edit in Workbench option that appears after generating, or upload files from your computer. You can drag motion cards (title cards, caption strips, transitions and about 150 demo animation cards) onto the timeline, trim, split, change speed, adjust opacity and position, and change card text and colors. An AI chat called 'Edit with AI' applies edits you describe in plain language, and every AI edit can be undone. Export video renders an MP4 in your own browser and saves it to your library. The older CineGen Studio route (#/cinegen) now opens the Workbench. Note: Workbench is a timeline editor; it is not a node graph for chaining generation steps.
Best for:
Creators who already have clips, images and audio from the other SmartVideo studios and want to assemble, caption and polish them into a finished video without leaving the app.
When to use it:
- You generated several clips or images in other studios and want to combine them into one video.

chunks.title: Workbench — Overview
chunks.text:
- You want to add title cards, captions, transitions or motion effects from the Motion library.
- You want to add or adjust sound: your own audio, the project's audio or background music options.
- You want to trim, split, speed up or slow down clips (speed 0.25x to 4x).
- You want to tell an AI 'trim the first clip to 3 seconds' or 'add a title card that says Hello' and have it applied for you.
- You want to export a finished MP4 from your browser.
When to use another studio:
- Use Timeline (#/timeline) when you want the full cut-and-export editor with its own AI chat modes (Ask, Search, Cut, Timeline); note Workbench is not the editor used for Director, Timeline or Video Agent results.
- Use Director (#/director) when you want AI agents to analyse or cut an existing video (subtitles, highlights, dubbing).
- Use Video Agent (#/video-agent) when you want a coded motion-graphics animation created from a prompt.
- Use Motion Director (#/motion-director) when you want a promo film planned from your website; it has its own editor.
- Use Video (#/video), Image (#/image) or Audio (#/audio) first when you do not have any media yet.
- Use Library (#/library) to find and manage your past generations.

chunks.title: Workbench — How to use
chunks.text:
Workbench (#/workbench). How to use.
How to use:
1. Open Workbench from the Agents group in the side menu (#/workbench). Or click Edit in Workbench in a studio's generation notification. 2. Click + Add your generations, select the videos, images or audio you want and click Add to timeline. You can also use Upload from computer in the Media tab. 3. Click an item in the Media, Motion, Sound or Themes tabs to preview it, and drag it onto a track to add it. 4. Click a clip on the timeline and use Properties to change text, colors, Start, Duration, Speed, Opacity, Scale and position. 5. Drag clip edges to trim, press S to split at the playhead, Ctrl/Cmd+D to duplicate, Delete to remove. 6. To edit by chatting, open Edit with AI, type an instruction such as 'Trim the first clip to 3 seconds' and send it; press Ctrl/Cmd+Z if you do not like the result. 7. Press Space to play the preview. 8. Click Export video, wait for 'Exporting N%' to finish and download the MP4 (it is also saved to your library).
Steps:
- Open Workbench or choose Edit in Workbench from a generation notification.
- Add media with + Add your generations or Upload from computer.
- Add motion cards and sound by dragging from the library onto tracks.
- Select clips and fine-tune them in Properties.
- Trim, split and rearrange on the timeline.
- Optionally ask Edit with AI to make changes.
- Preview with Space.

chunks.title: Workbench — How to use
chunks.text:
- Click Export video and download the MP4.
Getting started:
- Generate a couple of images or clips in other studios first so you have something to add.
- Click + Add your generations, pick them and add them to the timeline.
- Try the suggestion buttons in Edit with AI to see how chat editing works.
- Learn four shortcuts: Space, S, Delete, Ctrl/Cmd+Z.
Tips:
- Hover Motion thumbnails to see them animate.
- Use Fit to see the whole timeline.
- Use Hide track to check what is underneath.
- Use Export JSON before big experiments.
Best practices:
- Name your project at the top so exports are easy to find.
- Keep text on top tracks and footage underneath.
- Make AI edits one at a time so you can undo cleanly.
- Keep the tab open during export.

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text:
Workbench (#/workbench). Features.
Key features:
- Multi-track timeline: upper tracks cover lower ones; drag clips, trim both ends, split, duplicate, move between tracks.
- Library tabs: Media, Motion, Sound and Themes. Click an item to preview it; drag it onto the timeline to add it.
- Motion cards: native text card, Ink Press title card, narration caption strip, warm-white flash transition and about 150 demo animation cards in categories.
- Properties inspector: Content & style, Timing & speed (Start, Duration, Speed, In point), Layer (Opacity, Scale, Offset X, Offset Y).
- Live preview with play controls; the preview matches the final render.
- Edit with AI chat using your own OpenAI key; every AI edit can be undone.
- + Add your generations picker for images, videos and audio you made in SmartVideo studios.
- Upload from computer (video, image, audio) with size limits.
- Export video renders MP4 in your browser and saves it to your library.
- Export JSON and Import for the project file; Undo and Redo; Reset to the sample project.
- Interface language: English, Chinese or Russian.
- Autosave in your browser.
Feature details:

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text:
- feature: + Add your generations | explanation: A button in the bar above the editor opens a picker titled 'Add your generations' showing your recent generations (up to 120) as tiles with VIDEO, IMAGE or AUDIO badges. Click tiles to select them; the footer button reads 'Add to timeline' or 'Add N to timeline'. Close with the Close button. | whyToUse: Quickest way to bring work from other studios onto the timeline. | inputRequired: At least one saved generation. | restrictions: If you have none it says 'No generations yet. Create something in any AI studio (Image, Video, Cinema, Audio...) first.' Generations from Director, Timeline and Video Agent are not offered because those studios keep their own editors.
- feature: Edit in Workbench hand-off | explanation: After a studio finishes a generation, its notification can offer 'Edit in Workbench', which opens the Workbench with that result ready to add. The hand-off expires after 10 minutes. | whyToUse: Skip manual picking. | inputRequired: A finished generation. | restrictions: Not offered for Director, Timeline, Video Agent or Workbench's own exports.

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text: - feature: Library: Media, Motion, Sound, Themes | explanation: Media holds your imported clips and an 'Upload from computer' drop area. Motion lists motion cards (native cards first, then demo cards by category); thumbnails are still frames and play when you hover. Sound lists project audio and BGM options, with a 'Find sounds on Freesound' link. Themes holds color palettes you can apply and save, with Import palette and Export palette. Hint: 'Click to preview, drag onto the timeline'. | whyToUse: Everything you can add to your video lives here. | inputRequired: None. | restrictions: Cards marked 'tunable' have editable text and style fields; other demo cards can be trimmed, sped up, frozen and transformed but not re-worded. Some Sound features (such as project audio and Freesound downloading) belong to the developer workflow and may not apply to normal use.

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text:
- feature: Timeline | explanation: Toolbar buttons: Split (S) cuts the selected clip at the playhead, Duplicate (Ctrl/Cmd+D), Delete (Delete key), + Track (adds a track on top), Fit (zoom to fit) and a Zoom slider. Track headers let you drag to reorder, Hide track or Show track, and Delete track (asks for confirmation). Clips snap to other clips; drag the side handles to trim. | whyToUse: Assemble and refine your edit. | inputRequired: None. | restrictions: Clips on the same track may overlap; use more tracks for layering. Speed is a constant speed change (no speed curves).
- feature: Properties inspector | explanation: Select a clip to edit it. Content & style shows the card's own fields (text, colors, sizes). Timing & speed has Start, Duration, Speed, In point and a restore-original-duration button. Layer has Opacity, Scale, Offset X and Offset Y. A Delete clip button is at the bottom. | whyToUse: Precise control of each clip. | inputRequired: A selected clip. | restrictions: With nothing selected it says 'Select a clip on the timeline to edit its text, colors, animation timing, speed and layer.'

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text: - feature: Edit with AI (chat) | explanation: Describe an edit such as 'Cut the intro to 2s and add a caption "Summer sale"'. The AI replies briefly and returns edit operations (update a clip, set card text, add, remove, split or move clips, add or remove tracks, rename the project or set its background). The app checks every operation and applies only valid ones, then shows a note such as '2 changes applied - Ctrl/Cmd+Z to undo' and, if some were skipped, how many. While it works it shows 'Editing...'. Suggestion buttons include 'Trim the first clip to 3 seconds', 'Add a title card at the start that says "Hello"', 'Slow the second clip down to half speed' and 'Fade the music to 40% volume'. | whyToUse: Faster than clicking through panels for simple edits. | inputRequired: Your own OpenAI key saved in Settings and a message. | restrictions: Messages are cut at 4,000 characters, the last 12 chat turns are sent as history, and the project must be under about 200,000 characters of data ('Project is too large for AI editing.'). The AI can only reuse media files already in your project; it is told never to invent file addresses. Speed must stay between 0.25 and 4, opacity 0 to 1, durations at least 2 frames.

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text: - feature: Upload from computer | explanation: Drop or choose a video, image or audio file in the Media tab. It is stored so the clip keeps working after reload. The status text shows 'Uploading <name>...' then '<name> saved', or 'Couldn't save <name> - <reason>'. | whyToUse: Use your own footage, pictures or music. | inputRequired: A media file. | restrictions: Maximum sizes are 50 MB for video, 10 MB for images and 10 MB for audio. Wrong types show '<name> isn't a video, image or audio file.' and large files show '<name> is too large (max N MB for <type>).' Accepted extensions include mp4, mov, webm, m4v, mkv, ogv, 3gp (video), jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp, svg, bmp, avif, heic (image) and mp3, wav, aac, ogg, flac, m4a, opus, aiff, aif (audio).

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text:
- feature: Export video | explanation: The top bar Export video button renders the project to MP4 in your browser (tooltip 'Render the current project to MP4 in your browser'). It shows 'Exporting N%', then 'Exported - Download again'; on failure 'Export failed - Retry' or 'Export failed to start'. The finished MP4 is also uploaded to your library, with status text 'Saving export to your library...' then 'Export saved to your library'. | whyToUse: Get your finished video. | inputRequired: A project with clips. | restrictions: Runs in your browser tab, so keep it open. If the upload fails you see 'Export downloaded - couldn't save to library (<reason>)'.
- feature: Project tools | explanation: Project name (click to edit), Undo and Redo (Ctrl/Cmd+Z and Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Z), Export JSON, Import (project JSON) and Reset to sample. Interface language selector. Changes autosave in your browser. | whyToUse: Back up and manage your project. | inputRequired: A project JSON for Import. | restrictions: Invalid files show 'Import failed: not a valid project JSON'.
Modes:
- Manual timeline editing
- Edit with AI (chat edits)
- Library hand-off
Mode details:
- mode: Manual timeline editing | description: Drag, trim, split and adjust clips yourself. | useCase: Precise control.

chunks.title: Workbench — Features
chunks.text:
- mode: Edit with AI (chat edits) | description: You describe a change; the AI returns a list of validated edit operations that are applied to the project. | useCase: Quick structural or text changes.
- mode: Library hand-off | description: Generations arrive from + Add your generations or Edit in Workbench, either as a new project or appended to the current one. | useCase: Bringing in material from other studios.
Models:
Workbench itself does not generate images or video. Only the Edit with AI chat uses a model: it calls the OpenAI Responses API with your own OpenAI key. The default model in the code is gpt-5.6-sol, and a deployment can override it with the environment variable OPENAI_RESPONSES_TEXT_MODEL. The model returns a short reply plus a list of edit operations (update clip, set text props, add clip, remove clip, split clip, move to track, add or remove track, set project name or background). The app validates every operation before applying it. Rendering uses Remotion in your browser.

chunks.title: Workbench — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
Workbench (#/workbench). Problems and limits.
Troubleshooting:
- Editor area is blank or says 'Workbench is still loading...': wait a few seconds; if it persists reload the page.
- 'No generations yet': create something in an image, video, cinema or audio studio first, then reopen the picker.
- AI chat says it uses your own OpenAI key: save your OpenAI key in Settings, API keys (OpenAI API Key) and try again.
- AI chat says 'The AI returned an unreadable answer. Try rephrasing.': send the instruction again in simpler words.
- AI chat says 'AI request timed out': try again with a smaller project or a shorter instruction (the request limit is 60 seconds).
- Upload refused: check the file type and size (video 50 MB, image 10 MB, audio 10 MB).
- 'Export failed - Retry': click again, keep the tab open and reduce the project size.
- Status says 'Export downloaded - couldn't save to library': the MP4 downloaded but upload failed; keep the file and check your connection.
- 'Please sign in to SmartVid to use AI editing.': sign in again.
Troubleshooting steps:
- issue: AI chat does not edit anything | steps: Open Settings and confirm your OpenAI key is saved.; Make sure there are clips on the timeline for the AI to change.; Name the clip or track clearly in your instruction.; Read the note under the AI reply; skipped changes are counted there.

chunks.title: Workbench — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
- issue: My generation is not in the picker | steps: Check the generation was saved to your library.; Remember Director, Timeline and Video Agent results are excluded.; Reopen + Add your generations to refresh the list.
- issue: Export does not finish | steps: Keep the tab in front.; Click Export again after a failure.; Shorten the project or remove heavy cards, then retry.
Common problems:
- problem: I cannot change the text of a motion card | whyItHappens: Demo cards without the 'tunable' tag have no text fields. | howToFix: Use a native text card or a card marked tunable, or add a separate text card.
- problem: Clips overlap and one is hidden | whyItHappens: Upper tracks cover lower ones. | howToFix: Reorder tracks by dragging the handle, hide a track, or move the clip to another track.
- problem: The AI did not do what I asked | whyItHappens: Invalid edits are skipped. | howToFix: Press Ctrl/Cmd+Z, rephrase, or make the change manually.
Limitations:
- Edit with AI needs your own OpenAI key; there is no fallback platform key.
- Uploads are limited to 50 MB video, 10 MB image and 10 MB audio.
- AI chat cannot invent media; it only reuses files already in the project.
- Speed changes are constant (0.25x to 4x), with no speed curves.
- Demo motion cards cannot be re-worded; only 'tunable' cards have text and style fields.

chunks.title: Workbench — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
- Export runs in your browser and needs the tab to stay open.
- Director, Timeline and Video Agent results are not sent to Workbench.
- It is a timeline editor, not a node graph for chaining generations.
Limit details:
- limitation: AI chat needs an OpenAI key | impact: Without a key, chat replies with an error message instead of editing. | workaround: Add your OpenAI key in Settings, API keys, or edit manually.
- limitation: Large projects | impact: Very large projects return 'Project is too large for AI editing.' | workaround: Split work into smaller projects or edit manually.
- limitation: Upload size limits | impact: Big files are refused with a too-large message. | workaround: Compress or trim the file first, or use a generation from your library.
- limitation: Browser export | impact: Long or heavy projects export slowly. | workaround: Keep the tab open, close other heavy tabs, or shorten the project.
FAQs:
- question: Do I need an API key? | answer: Only for the Edit with AI chat, which uses your own OpenAI key. Manual editing and export need no key.
- question: Where does my export go? | answer: It is rendered in your browser, offered for download, and uploaded to your library.
- question: What happened to CineGen Studio? | answer: The #/cinegen address now opens the Workbench.
- question: Can I undo AI edits? | answer: Yes. Every AI edit can be undone with Ctrl/Cmd+Z.

chunks.title: Workbench — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
- question: How big can uploaded files be? | answer: Up to 50 MB for video, 10 MB for images and 10 MB for audio.
- question: Does my project save automatically? | answer: It autosaves in your browser. Use Export JSON for a backup file.

Workbench (#/workbench). Workflows and use cases.
Example workflows:
- title: Stitch three clips with a title | steps: Open Workbench and click + Add your generations.; Select three video tiles and click Add 3 to timeline.; Open the Motion tab, preview a title card and drag it to a top track at the start.; Edit its text in Properties under Content & style.; Click Export video and download the MP4.
- title: Fix pacing with AI chat | steps: Open Edit with AI.; Type 'Slow the second clip down to half speed' and send.; Check the note that says how many changes were applied.; Press Ctrl/Cmd+Z if you want to undo.
Use cases:
- title: Social video from AI shots | description: Combine several AI clips with captions and music. | steps: Add your clips and an audio file.; Add a caption card from the Motion tab.; Trim to a target length and export. | expectedOutput: A single MP4 ready to post.
- title: Photo slideshow with transitions | description: Make images flow with transition cards. | steps: Add images from your generations.; Place a transition card between clips.; Adjust durations in Properties. | expectedOutput: A slideshow MP4.
Related studios:
- studio: library | relationship: Your saved generations appear in the Workbench picker. | whenToMove: When you need to find or manage past generations. | why: Workbench only shows recent items from the library.

chunks.title: Workbench — Glossary
chunks.text: Glossary: Clip: One piece of media or one motion card placed on a track. | Track: A horizontal layer on the timeline. Upper tracks cover lower ones. | Playhead: The marker showing the current time. | Motion card: A ready-made animated element such as a title or transition. | Tunable: A card whose text and style can be edited in Properties. | In point: Where inside the source clip playback starts. | Theme: A saved color palette that restyles the project.

chunks.title: Which API keys the app uses (bring your own keys)
phrases: what api keys do I need
which key do I need for generation
do I need an openai key
why do I need my own api key
what is the videodb key for
chunks.text:
Which API keys the app uses (bring your own keys).
SmartVideo works on your own provider keys (bring-your-own-key). In Settings the key forms are: "Muapi API Key" (described as "Used for video generation and Muapi-powered effects."), "OpenAI API Key" ("Used for image and text generation via OpenAI models."), "VideoDB API Key" ("Used by the Timeline Editor, Video Agent, Render and Director for video indexing, search and retrieval via VideoDB."), and two optional stock-media keys, "Pexels API Key (optional)" and "Pixabay API Key (optional)". The server side states that there is no platform-key fallback: functions run on the keys your browser sends. In practice: the MuAPI key powers generation in the studios; the OpenAI key powers the AI features that call OpenAI, such as Ask SmartVideo, the Timeline AI tools, Director, Video Agent and Workbench. Without the right key those features ask you to add it.

chunks.title: How to add or change your API keys
phrases: where do I enter my api key
how do I set up my openai key
chunks.text:
How to add or change your API keys.
The key form is a popup titled "Welcome — set up your API keys" with the text "Add your provider API keys to create content. Each key is stored separately on this device. You can change these anytime from Settings." It opens by itself once per browser session when you land in the app with no keys saved. It also opens when you press Generate in a studio without a MuAPI key, and Ask SmartVideo shows an "Open Settings → API keys" button that opens it. Each provider has its own form: paste the key, press "Save Muapi API Key" or "Save OpenAI API Key" (the button reads "Saved ✓" when done), "Clear" to remove it, or "Test" to check it. Each form has a "Grab API Key" link that opens the provider page in a new tab (muapi.ai/access-keys for Muapi, platform.openai.com/login for OpenAI). "Skip for now" and "Done" close the popup. The header key icon (tooltip "Update API Key") clears your saved MuAPI key and reloads the page.

chunks.title: API key formats, checks and error messages
phrases: what does a muapi key look like
chunks.text:
API key formats, checks and error messages.
Placeholders in the forms: "sk-... (Muapi key)", "sk-... (OpenAI key)", "VideoDB access token", "Pexels API key" and "Pixabay API key". Before saving, the form checks the format: no spaces ("contains spaces — copy the key without any extra characters"), not pasted twice ("looks duplicated — it appears to be pasted twice. Paste it once."), and at least 10 characters ("appears too short"). Leaving the box empty and saving clears the key. The server accepts an OpenAI key that starts with "sk-" followed by at least 20 letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, and a MuAPI key of 16 to 200 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens. Messages you may see: "This uses your own MuAPI key. Add it in SmartVid → Settings → API keys (MuAPI API Key)."; "OpenAI rejected your API key. Check it in SmartVid → Settings → API keys."; "Your OpenAI account is rate-limited or out of credit. Check your OpenAI billing, then try again."; "MuAPI rejected your API key, or the account is out of credit. Check it in SmartVid → Settings → API keys." Never share your key in chat or screenshots.

chunks.title: Where your API keys are stored
phrases: where is my api key stored
how to delete my api key
key not saved on another device
chunks.text:
Where your API keys are stored.
Keys you save are kept in your own browser on this device, per provider. When you press Save, the key is stored for the current tab session (session storage) and also persisted in the browser (local storage), lightly obfuscated rather than strongly encrypted, according to the code comments. Because they live in your browser, a key saved in one browser or device does not appear in another, and clearing site data removes it. The browser sends the key with each request that needs it (headers X-MuAPI-Key and X-OpenAI-Key) and the server code says keys are never logged or stored. Use the Clear button in Settings to remove a key. Use a key you can revoke at the provider if you ever suspect it leaked.

chunks.title: What Ask SmartVideo is and how to use it
phrases: how do I use the help assistant
how to get help in the app
the assistant asks me to sign in
chunks.text:
What Ask SmartVideo is and how to use it.
Ask SmartVideo is the floating help assistant, opened with the "Ask SmartVideo" launcher button. It answers questions about the studios and points you to the right one with source chips such as "Open <studio>". The header shows "You're in <studio>" when you are inside a studio, or "Help for every studio". It uses retrieved help content and your own OpenAI key: if none is saved it shows "Ask SmartVideo uses your own OpenAI key." with an "Open Settings → API keys" button. You must be signed in ("Sign in to use Ask SmartVideo."), and asking too fast gives "You are asking too fast. Please wait a moment." Type in the box ("Ask about any studio…", up to 1500 characters), press Enter to send and Shift+Enter for a new line. Esc closes the panel and "Clear" erases the conversation. The conversation is kept for the browser tab only.

chunks.title: Signing in, signing up and resetting your password
chunks.text:
Signing in, signing up and resetting your password.
Accounts are handled by Clerk. The pages are /signin, /signup, /forgot-password, /reset-password, /account and /profile. Sign in shows "Welcome Back / Sign in to continue your creative journey" with email, password, "Remember me", "Forgot password?" and a "Sign In" button. Sign up shows "Start Your Journey / Create your account and start creating" with full name, email and password, then "Create Account"; next you get "Verify Your Email" where you enter the 6-digit code emailed to you, then "Verify Email". Password reset works by an emailed code: open "Forgot password?", enter your email, then follow the code and new-password steps. Errors show messages such as "Sign in failed. Please check your credentials." The header shows a "Sign In" link when you are signed out.

chunks.title: Your account and profile pages
phrases: how do I change my password
where do I see my email
chunks.text:
Your account and profile pages.
When signed in, the header shows your email address (on wide screens) and a user menu with "Profile", "Account" and "Sign out". The Account page (/account) shows your avatar, "Profile Information" (Full Name, Username, Member since), "Email Addresses" with a Verified or Unverified tag, "Quick Links" (Edit Profile and Change Password) and a "Sign Out" section. Change Password sends you to the forgot-password flow. The Profile page (/profile) says "Manage your account details, security, and preferences." and embeds the account manager for editing details. If you open these pages while signed out you are shown the sign-in (or sign-up) page. Billing and subscription management screens are not described in the repository.

chunks.title: Which actions need a plan with full access
phrases: why does it say upgrade to access this feature
which features need a paid plan
do I need to pay to use upscale
chunks.text:
Which actions need a plan with full access.
The app checks for a feature named "smartvideo_full_access" through your account (a billing entitlement) or a legacy-access flag on the account. If you are signed out or lack it, certain actions stop with the toast "Upgrade to access this feature". In the code these checks run when you press Generate or similar actions in Upscale Suite, Effects Studio, Avatar Studio, Character Studio, Storyboard Studio (generating frames and exporting PDF), Render (actions) and Director (each command; its message says "This feature requires an active subscription. Please check your plan in Settings."). Other studios such as Image Studio and Video Studio do not show this check in the code reviewed. Separately you still need your own MuAPI key for generation. Exact plan tiers and what each includes in the product are not documented beyond the offer text.

chunks.title: The Lifetime and Whitelabel offers as shown on the landing page
chunks.text:
The Lifetime and Whitelabel offers as shown on the landing page.
The landing page offer is "Get Lifetime Access Today" with the line "Pay once, own forever. No subscriptions, no hidden fees." Two plans: "Lifetime Access" at $199, "One-time payment • Forever yours", which lists full access to all 34 AI Creative Apps, all 60+ AI Features & Capabilities, a 200+ AI Models Library, Commercial Usage Rights, Priority Support Access and Lifetime Updates, with a "30-day money-back guarantee". "Whitelabel Pro" at $997, "One-time payment • Full ownership", labelled "Most Popular" and "Everything in Lifetime, plus": Your Own Branding (remove all watermarks and use custom logos), Resell Rights, Whitelabel Domain, Priority GPU+ (10x faster rendering speeds), Unlimited Clients, API Access, Custom Workflows and Dedicated Support (24/7 priority assistance), with "30-day money-back guarantee • Instant delivery". Checkout buttons read "Get Lifetime Access — $199" and "Get Whitelabel Pro — $997". This is marketing copy from the page; it does not describe credits, usage limits or team seats.

chunks.title: The side menu and how to navigate
phrases: how do I open video studio
how do I find the courses
chunks.text:
The side menu and how to navigate.
The left side menu is the main way to move around (on phones it opens with the menu button at the top left). It has five groups. Top, with no heading: Apps, Explore, Templates, Academy (courses and guides). Image: Image, Edit, Upscale, Character, Product Shot, Brand. Video: Video, Cinema, Cinema Templates, Storyboard, Effects, AI VFX, Animate, Lip Sync, Video Tools, Avatar, Audio. Agents: Video Agent, Director, Timeline, Workbench, Viral, Personalizer, Website. My Work: Library, Content. The current page is highlighted. The Apps page lists the same tools as cards with a search box, and clicking the logo at the top left of the header opens Apps. Pages use addresses like #/image. Some routes are part of a menu entry: for example Brand DNA, Campaign and Photo Studio belong to Brand, and text-to-image or image-to-image belong to Image.

chunks.title: Chat, Assist, Training and Community pages were retired
phrases: what happened to the assist page
chunks.text:
Chat, Assist, Training and Community pages were retired.
Several older pages no longer exist and old links redirect to the closest live page: Training, Chat and Assist open the Apps hub; Community opens Explore; and the old pexels-media page opens Library. If you were looking for a chat assistant, use Ask SmartVideo (the floating help button) for questions about the app, or the Video Agent and Director apps for AI-driven video work. Stock photos and videos from Pexels are now reached through "Browse Stock Media" on the Content page.

chunks.title: Where your generated files are saved
phrases: how do I download my image
chunks.text:
Where your generated files are saved.
Everything you create in any studio is saved automatically in Library (side menu, My Work group), which shows your images, videos and audio and a separate Uploads view of files you uploaded. History is merged from cloud storage and your browser, and when a MuAPI key is saved MuAPI's own history is added too. In Library you can Download, Copy prompt, Save (to Content) or Delete an item. Content is the shelf for items you chose to keep: saved generations, uploads, PDFs and Pexels stock media. Saved items in Content are stored in your browser. How long generated links stay valid and storage limits are not stated in the code.

chunks.title: The balance chip in the header
phrases: what is the number in the top bar
how much credit do I have
where do I see my balance
chunks.text:
The balance chip in the header.
In the top bar the app shows a small rounded chip with a dollar amount such as "$12.34". Its tooltip is "MuAPI credit balance". It reads the balance of your MuAPI account, so it needs a saved MuAPI key; until a balance has been read, or if it cannot be read, the chip stays hidden. It refreshes after each finished generation and when you return to the browser tab (at most once every 30 seconds). The code does not say how credits are priced per model, how to top up or how billing works; top-ups are handled with your MuAPI account, which is not documented in this app.

chunks.title: Choosing a model in a studio
phrases: how do I choose a model
why is my model not available
chunks.text:
Choosing a model in a studio.
Most generation studios have a model picker next to the prompt so you can choose which AI model makes the result. The list depends on the studio and the task: for example the Apps hub badges say Image Studio has 20+ models and Video Studio 15+ models. In Template Studio the picker shows "Model · <route>" (for example Image → Video) and only offers models that accept the media you attached; if the chosen model is not compatible it falls back to the first model for that route and says so. Some studios show an estimated cost line like "≈ 5 USD" beside Generate when the estimate is available; it is best-effort and simply hidden if unavailable. Model-by-model quality comparisons are not described in the app.

chunks.title: Prompt and keyboard tips that exist in the app
phrases: how to write a good prompt
how do I submit with the keyboard
chunks.text:
Prompt and keyboard tips that exist in the app.
In studios that use the floating prompt composer (for example Video Studio, Cinema Studio, Effects Studio and Video Tools) the box says "Describe what you want to create" and pressing Ctrl+Enter (or Cmd+Enter on Mac) submits like the Generate button. Esc closes open pop-overs. Explore has a Prompt Library of 12 sample prompts with a "Try this prompt" button that opens Image Studio with the prompt filled in. Template Studio keeps an "AI Enhancer" switch ON by default, which expands short prompts, and shows the final text in the "Enhanced Prompt" tab. Ask SmartVideo uses Enter to send and Shift+Enter for a new line. The Timeline editor Settings has a Keyboard tab; its listed defaults include Space for Play/Pause, Home and End to jump, Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo, S to split a clip and Ctrl+E to export.

chunks.title: Using the app on phones and which browsers work
phrases: can I use it on my iphone
chunks.text:
Using the app on phones and which browsers work.
On small screens the side menu is hidden and opens with a menu button fixed at the top left ("Toggle navigation menu"); tapping outside it closes it. Ask SmartVideo becomes a full-screen panel on phones. The app repository does not publish a user-facing list of supported browsers. An internal staging checklist lists Chrome, Firefox and Safari (latest two stable versions) as the test targets, and browser-side video processing needs MediaRecorder support, otherwise it reports "MediaRecorder/captureStream unsupported in this browser". For the most reliable experience use a current desktop version of Chrome, Firefox or Safari and keep browser storage enabled, since keys and some history are kept there.

chunks.title: What the help content does not cover
phrases: how much does each generation cost
how do I buy more credits
chunks.text:
What the help content does not cover.
The documentation in this app does not describe: how credits are priced per generation or per model, how to buy or top up credits, refund or billing procedures beyond the "30-day money-back guarantee" line on the offer, team or multi-seat features (the Whitelabel offer mentions "Unlimited Clients" and "Resell Rights" only as marketing lines), usage limits per plan, or the data-retention period for generated files. If you ask about these, the honest answer is that it is not documented here and you should check your account or contact support through the channel you purchased from. Ask SmartVideo can only explain what is in the app and its help content.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works (AI Video Ads & UGC).
A UGC ad is just five pieces stitched together — once you can see the seams, you can make any of them.

Track: AI Video Ads & UGC
Time: ~45 minutes
Prerequisites: None

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / The Problem (AI Video Ads & UGC).
Brands pay real creators $200-$1,500 per UGC (user-generated-content-style) ad because it converts better than polished studio ads — it looks like a real person talking to camera about a product, not a commercial. The problem: sourcing, briefing, filming, and revising human creators is slow, and it doesn't scale. A brand that wants 20 ad variants to test can't get 20 creators on short notice.

AI-generated UGC solves the scaling problem, but most people trying it get stuck on one thing: their AI "creator" doesn't look consistent from shot to shot, or the voice/lip-sync looks obviously fake, and the ad gets rejected. Understanding the actual pipeline — not just "type a prompt" — is what separates a usable ad from an uncanny one.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / The Concept (AI Video Ads & UGC).
A UGC-style AI ad is five stages, each producible independently and swappable:

Script  →  Avatar / Voice  →  Video  →  Captions  →  Export

- Script — a short, conversational hook + pitch + call-to-action, written the way a real person talks, not ad copy.
- Avatar/Voice — either a generated talking-head avatar with a cloned/synthetic voice, or a still reference image animated with lip-sync driven by an audio track.
- Video — the avatar's performance, plus any b-roll (product shots, screen recordings) cut around it.
- Captions — auto-generated, burned-in captions, standard for the format because most viewers watch muted.
- Export — format/aspect ratio matched to the platform (9:16 for Reels/TikTok/Shorts, sometimes 1:1 or 16:9).

The reason this pipeline matters more than any single "best model" is that each stage can be produced by a different tool, and the weak link is whichever stage looks least real — usually the avatar's face/voice sync, not the script or captions.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Do It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Write the script. Keep it under 30 seconds spoken (~75-90 words). Structure: hook (first 2 seconds — a question, a bold claim, or a visual surprise), problem/pitch (10-15 seconds), proof or demo (10-15 seconds), call-to-action (last 2-3 seconds).
2. Generate the voice. Use a text-to-speech or voice-cloning model to turn the script into natural-sounding narration. Match tone to the product (energetic for a gadget, calm for skincare) — and don't stop at the first take. Generate 2-3 versions varying pacing and emphasis (which word gets stressed in the hook line changes how "surprised" or "casual" it reads), and pick the one that sounds least like it's being read off a page. Accent/demographic match to the product's likely audience matters here too — a mismatched voice can undercut an otherwise good script.
3. Generate or animate the avatar. Either generate a talking-head video directly from the script/voice, or animate a reference image with lip-sync driven by the audio track.
4. Add b-roll. Cut in product shots or screen recordings during the pitch/proof section — this also hides any short imperfect stretches in the avatar footage.
5. Caption and export. Auto-generate captions, burn them in, and export at 9:16 for short-form platforms.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Do It
chunks.text: 6. Ship check. Before sending anything to a client, watch the finished ad once with sound off (does the hook work from captions alone?) and once with sound on at regular volume. If you catch yourself pausing anywhere to figure out what's happening, a client will too — that's a sign to fix pacing or cut, not just ship it and see.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Worked Example (AI Video Ads & UGC).

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Worked Example
chunks.text: - Proof/Demo (15-25s): a visual demo (slapping the phone on) plus a concrete duration ("two weeks, potholes included") — specific numbers read as more credible than "it works great." - CTA (25-28s): price stated plainly, one action ("link's below"), urgency tied to a real use case (road trip) instead of a generic "buy now." Why this script would survive production: it's short enough to keep energy up on one take, the demo moment (slapping the phone on) gives the avatar something to do with its hands instead of just talking — which also hides minor avatar imperfections — and it never says "AI" or sounds scripted. Common first-attempt mistake: writing the pitch section like copy ("Introducing GripMount, the revolutionary new way to...") instead of like speech. Read your script out loud before producing anything — if you wouldn't say it to a friend, rewrite it. The clip below is real, not a mockup — the anchor image from Module 2 animated into a short talking clip from the hook line above, so you can see what a first-pass output actually looks like before any editing/b-roll/captions are added:

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Worked Example
chunks.text:
How this was actually produced, end to end, via the muapi API:
1. Generated the anchor portrait with nano-banana-2 (text-to-image, $0.06/image) — the same image used in Module 2's example.
2. Uploaded that image via muapi's uploadfile endpoint to get a URL the next model could reference.
3. Fed that image URL into seedance-2-image-to-video-fast (image-to-video, $0.75/clip) with a prompt describing the action and the exact line of dialogue — no separate TTS/lip-sync pass was needed, since this model generates speech and mouth movement together from the prompt.
4. Downloaded the resulting .mp4 from muapi's CDN (generated outputs expire after 30 days, so anything you want to keep needs downloading promptly) and converted it to the silent GIF preview above with ffmpeg for inline display.

Total cost for this one clip: $0.81 across the two model calls. This is exactly the "image → video model, prompt-driven" pipeline described in Do It, step 3 — the models named here are current examples, not a fixed recommendation; see Compare Tools below for how to pick a model when these become outdated.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Compare Tools (AI Video Ads & UGC).
Model names change constantly, but the category choice matters more than any specific model — here's what's actually reasonable for each stage right now:

| Stage | Good muapi models to reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Voice/TTS | Gemini TTS, ElevenLabs text-to-dialogue | Natural multi-speaker delivery with emotion/pace control — not robotic TTS |
| Avatar/video (image → talking clip) | Seedance 2.x, Kling 3.0 | Current-generation video models that handle head/hand motion and speech convincingly in one pass, as in the clip above |
| Lip-sync (audio-driven, onto an existing video/image) | A dedicated lip-sync model (e.g. sync-style lip-sync) or a Kling avatar model | Better fit when you already have separately-recorded narration you need to match to a face, rather than generating speech+motion together |

| Path | Cost per ad | Setup effort | Consistency | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| muapi API (managed) | Per-generation credit cost, no infra | Low — call the endpoint, get a result | High — same model/voice reused via API params | Fast iteration, client work, testing many variants |
| Other paid all-in-one UGC tools | Often subscription-gated, per-seat pricing | Low, but locked to their UI/workflow | Varies by tool | Teams that want a GUI, not an API |

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
| Local/self-hosted (ComfyUI + local TTS/video models, e.g. LTX 2.3) | Free after hardware, but needs a capable GPU | High — workflow setup, model downloads, tuning | Can be very high once tuned, but slower to get there | Zero marginal cost at volume, full control, privacy-sensitive clients who don't want cloud processing |

LTX 2.3 is worth naming specifically for the local path: it's an open-weight video model runnable in ComfyUI, so it's the closest local equivalent to the Seedance/Kling-class models above — weaker out of the box, but the only one of this group you can actually run on your own GPU instead of an API call.

The honest tradeoff: local is genuinely free per-generation once set up, but the setup and iteration time cost is real — expect to spend a weekend tuning a ComfyUI workflow before it's reliable. API is the right default while you're still learning what "good" looks like; local becomes worth it once you're producing at real volume (dozens of ads/month) or a client specifically needs on-premise generation.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Launch It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Launch It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
How to price it: Individual UGC-style ad gigs on freelance marketplaces run roughly $10-$55 per finished ad; agencies retainer this work at $1,500-$3,000/month for ongoing batches. Price by deliverable (e.g., "$150 for 5 ad variants") rather than by hour — clients understand ad packages, not your production time.

How to position it: Lead with the business outcome ("more ad variants to test, faster, without a film crew"), not the AI process. Brands buying UGC ads care about conversion and testing speed, not how the video was made.

Where to find first clients: DTC e-commerce brands running paid social ads are the best fit — they already buy UGC and already understand the format. Cold outreach to brands you can see running Meta/TikTok ads (visible in the platforms' public ad libraries) with a sample ad for their actual product is a stronger opener than a generic pitch.

The real numbers: Documented case studies show individual brands running AI-UGC-style creative at $600K+/month in ad spend for a single product — the point isn't that you'll match that, it's that the format is proven at scale, not a novelty.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Exercises
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Exercises (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Easy: Write three 30-second UGC scripts for a product you use, following the hook/pitch/proof/CTA structure.
2. Medium: Produce one full ad end-to-end (script → voice → avatar → captions → export) for a real or hypothetical product.
3. Hard: Produce 5 variants of the same ad (same product, different hooks or angles) and compare which hook you'd expect to perform best, and why.

chunks.text:

- templates/ugc-script-template.md — the hook/pitch/proof/CTA script structure as a fill-in-the-blank template.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency (AI Video Ads & UGC).
If your AI creator looks like a different person in every shot, nobody will pay for the ad.

Track: AI Video Ads & UGC
Time: ~40 minutes
Prerequisites: How AI UGC Actually Works

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / The Problem (AI Video Ads & UGC).
This is the single most common complaint from people trying AI-generated content: the same "character" comes out looking like a slightly different person in every generation — different face shape, different age, different outfit continuity. For a one-off image this doesn't matter. For a UGC ad campaign, a faceless channel host, or an AI influencer, it's disqualifying — viewers notice immediately, and clients will reject the work.

Most tutorials skip this because it's the hardest part to explain simply, and it's exactly why this is its own module rather than a footnote.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / The Concept (AI Video Ads & UGC).
Consistency comes from giving the model an "anchor" it can't drift away from, instead of re-describing the character in text every time. Three anchor types, from weakest to strongest:

- Prompt-only consistency — describing the character in detail every time (hair, face, age, clothing). Weakest — text descriptions are ambiguous and the model fills gaps differently each generation.
- Reference-image consistency — feeding a reference photo of the character alongside the prompt, so the model conditions on the actual face, not just a text description. Much stronger, and the easiest to use with API-based models.
- Fine-tuned/locked identity (LoRA or equivalent) — training a small adapter on multiple photos of the same character so the model can reproduce that exact identity from any prompt. Strongest and most portable across scenes, but requires more setup (usually a local/self-hosted step, not a single API call).

A fixed seed (the random-number starting point for generation) also helps within a single session, but seed-locking alone doesn't survive across different prompts or sessions the way a reference image or trained identity does — treat seed-locking as a helper, not the main mechanism.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Do It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Pick or generate your anchor character — either an AI-generated "founder" image or a stand-in reference photo, at high resolution, front-facing, neutral lighting.
2. Use reference-image conditioning for every subsequent generation of that character — pass the anchor image alongside each new prompt (different outfit, pose, background) rather than re-describing the person in text.
3. Check for drift — generate 3-5 variations and compare: same facial structure, same apparent age, consistent identifying features (freckles, specific hairstyle). If it's drifting, tighten the prompt to describe only what should change (outfit, background) and rely on the reference image for everything about the face.
4. For heavy repeat use (a recurring ad character, an influencer, a channel host), consider training a dedicated identity model (LoRA-style) — one-time setup cost, then near-perfect consistency across unlimited future generations.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Worked Example (AI Video Ads & UGC).

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Worked Example
chunks.text:
With reference-image conditioning: pass the anchor image alongside each new prompt ("same woman, now in a car, holding a phone" — describing only what changes). Face shape, freckles, and apparent age stay locked because the model is conditioning on the actual image, not re-guessing from text. This is the default that would work for a one-off GripMount client ad.

Drift-check, actually run — the anchor woman generated in 3 real settings (car interior, kitchen counter, walking outside), using the anchor image as a reference input to an edit-capable image model rather than a plain text prompt:

What actually happened: no meaningful drift across any of the 3 — face shape, freckle pattern, and hair all hold up even in the outdoor shot with completely different lighting than the anchor. This is the real result of reference-image conditioning done right: pass the anchor image as an edit input (not just describe the character in a fresh text prompt) and let the prompt describe only the setting. If you do see drift in your own attempts — a rounder jaw, vanished freckles, a different apparent age — it's usually because the prompt re-described facial features instead of only the surroundings, or the reference image wasn't actually passed to an edit-capable endpoint.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Worked Example
chunks.text:
When it's worth training a LoRA instead: if this same "creator" is going to front dozens of ads over months (not just one GripMount batch), a one-time LoRA training pass on 15-20 photos of her locks the identity in even more tightly and removes any per-shot risk at all — worth the setup once reuse, not one-off work, is the plan.

How the 3 shots above were produced: uploaded the anchor image once via muapi's uploadfile, then made 3 separate calls to nano-banana-2-edit ($0.06/image), passing that same uploaded image as the reference (imageslist) each time with a prompt describing only the new setting ("same woman as in the reference image, now sitting in a car...") — never re-describing the face itself. Other reference-conditioned edit models that work the same way: nano-banana-pro-edit, gpt-image-2-image-to-image.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Compare Tools (AI Video Ads & UGC).
For the reference-image step itself, current-generation image models (e.g. Nano Banana 2/Pro, Seedream) hold facial identity noticeably better across prompt changes than older-generation image models — the anchor portrait used in the Worked Example above came from one of these. Model quality matters more here than almost anywhere else in the pipeline, since this whole module exists to fight identity drift.

| Path | Consistency strength | Setup effort | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| muapi API, reference-image conditioning | Good — strong resemblance across generations | Low — pass a reference image param | Most UGC/ad work; fastest path to "good enough" |
| Other paid tools with built-in "character" features | Varies — some wrap reference-image conditioning behind a simpler UI | Low | Teams wanting a GUI over the same underlying technique |
| Local (ComfyUI + trained LoRA, or LTX 2.3 for the video side) | Strongest — near-identical identity across any prompt/scene | High — needs a training pass on multiple reference photos, then a workflow to use it | A recurring character used across dozens/hundreds of generations (an influencer, a channel host) where the training cost pays for itself |

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Compare Tools
chunks.text: Be honest with yourself about how many times you'll reuse this character. Reference-image conditioning via API is the right default for a one-off client ad. A trained local identity is worth the extra setup only once you're generating the same character repeatedly.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Launch It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Launch It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
How to price it: Consistency work isn't billed separately — it's what makes the deliverable usable at all, so it's baked into your ad or content pricing (see Module 4). What you can upsell is a "branded AI character" package — designing and locking a consistent identity a client can reuse across all future content, priced as a one-time setup fee ($200-$500) plus per-piece production after.

How to position it: Frame it as "your reusable AI spokesperson," not "an AI-generated photo." Clients pay more for something they can reuse across campaigns than for a single image.

Where this shows up: Every track in this curriculum depends on this module — an AI influencer, a faceless channel's "host," and a UGC ad character are all the same underlying consistency problem applied to a different business model.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Exercises
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Exercises (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Easy: Generate the same character in 3 different outfits using reference-image conditioning; check for facial drift across them.
2. Medium: Generate the same character in 5 different scenes/backgrounds and identify which details drift first (usually: age, specific facial proportions, hairstyle).
3. Hard: Set up a local ComfyUI workflow with a trained identity for one character and compare consistency against the API reference-image approach for the same 5 scenes.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / The Problem (AI Video Ads & UGC).
A single ad, however good, is a gamble on one hook and one angle. Brands that run paid social know this — they test multiple variants against each other and keep whichever performs. This is why the real service isn't "make me an ad," it's "make me 10 ad variants I can test" — and producing a batch efficiently, rather than one at a time from scratch, is what makes this a viable business rather than a slow craft.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / The Concept (AI Video Ads & UGC).
A batch isn't 10 unrelated ads — it's one product, varied along a small number of axes, so you can produce it efficiently while still giving the client meaningfully different things to test:

- Hook variation — same product, different opening 2 seconds (question, bold claim, before/after, problem-first)
- Angle variation — same product, different selling angle (price, convenience, social proof, novelty)
- Format variation — same script, different avatar/voice or b-roll style

Varying all three per ad would make every ad different in every way, making it impossible to know why one outperformed another. Vary one or two axes at a time and hold the rest constant — that's what makes the results the client gets back actually useful, not just "another ad."

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Do It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Lock the constants. Same product, same core proof point, same CTA — these stay fixed across the whole batch.
2. Write 3-4 hook variants using the script template from Module 1, each testing a different opening angle.
3. Pair hooks with 2-3 angle variants (price-focused, convenience-focused, social-proof-focused) to generate your combination matrix — e.g. 4 hooks × 3 angles doesn't mean 12 ads; pick the most promising 8-10 combinations rather than every permutation.
4. Reuse your consistent character (Module 2) across the whole batch unless the brief calls for multiple creator "types."
5. Batch-produce voice and avatar generation — since script/character are locked, this step is mostly repetition with different script text, which is where API-based generation earns its keep over one-by-one manual tools.
6. Deliver with a simple test plan — label each ad by which axis it varies, so the client (or you) can actually read the results afterward.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Worked Example (AI Video Ads & UGC).

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Worked Example
chunks.text:
Only the hook and opening angle change — product demo, proof section, and CTA stay identical across all 5, so if one ad wins, you know it's the hook, not some other variable.

Ad 1 (Module 1) vs. Ad 2 and Ad 3, actually generated — same anchor character (Module 2), same product, only the opening line changes. This is what "batching" looks like in practice, not just a table of hooks:

Producing these 3 took re-using the same uploaded anchor image across 3 separate seedance-2-image-to-video-fast calls, changing only the prompt's dialogue line each time (~$0.75/clip) — this is exactly what "batch-produce voice and avatar generation" in Do It, step 5 means: the character and product stay fixed, only the script text changes per call.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Worked Example
chunks.text:
How to actually read the test once these are running as paid social ads: check hook rate first (the % of viewers who watch past the first 2-3 seconds) — an ad with a weak hook rate is dead regardless of anything downstream, so don't bother comparing CPA on it yet. Only compare cost-per-result (CPA/ROAS) across ads that already have a decent hook rate; a low CPA on very little spend is noise, not a signal. A common rule of thumb: run each variant long enough to clear a few thousand impressions (roughly 3-4 days at a modest daily budget per variant) before calling a winner — long enough to get past the platform's initial learning phase, short enough not to waste spend on an obvious loser.

Labeling for the client: deliver the batch with each ad tagged by which single thing it varies ("Ad 2 = problem-first hook") so whoever's running the media buy can read the result back to a specific creative decision, not just "ad 2 did better."

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Compare Tools (AI Video Ads & UGC).
| Path | Throughput for a 10-ad batch | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| muapi API | Fast — script the batch as repeated calls varying only script text/params | Client work with deadlines; the default for batch production |
| Other paid UGC tools (GUI-based) | Slower — usually one-at-a-time through a UI, even if the UI is polished | Occasional single ads, not batch production |
| Local/self-hosted | Can be fast once a batch-generation workflow is set up (e.g. a ComfyUI workflow queue), but the setup investment only pays off at high recurring volume | Agencies producing many batches per month who've already paid the local setup cost in Module 1/2 |

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Launch It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Launch It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
How to price it: Price per batch, not per ad — e.g. "$150-$300 for a 5-8 ad test batch," scaling with revisions included. This matches how brands already think about UGC ad budgets and is easier to sell than a per-ad rate card.

How to position it: Sell the testing capability, not the ad count — "get 8 variants to find your winner" is a stronger pitch than "get 8 ads." Brands running paid social already understand why this matters.

Where to find first clients: Same as Module 1 — DTC brands visibly running paid social ads. For batch work specifically, mention in outreach that you can turn around a full test batch faster than sourcing multiple human creators, since speed-to-test is the actual value prop here.

The real numbers: Agency-level UGC ad retainers documented in the $1,500-$3,000/month range are typically buying ongoing batch production like this, not one-off ads — this module is what makes that retainer model deliverable.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Exercises
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Exercises (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Easy: Plan a 6-ad batch matrix (3 hooks × 2 angles) for a product of your choice, without producing it yet.
2. Medium: Produce a 5-ad batch end-to-end, holding character and CTA constant while varying hook and angle.
3. Hard: Produce a 10-ad batch and write a one-page "test plan" a client could use to track which variant performed best.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service (AI Video Ads & UGC).
The production is the easy part now. Getting paid for it is a different skill.

Track: AI Video Ads & UGC
Time: ~35 minutes
Prerequisites: How AI UGC Actually Works, Building a 10-Ad Batch

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / The Problem (AI Video Ads & UGC).
Most people who can produce good AI UGC ads still make far less than they could, because they price by guessing, undersell out of fear of rejection, or pitch the technology instead of the result. Meanwhile the actual market — freelance gigs and agency retainers — already has established price ranges you can anchor to instead of guessing.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / The Concept (AI Video Ads & UGC).
There are three ways to sell this, each with a different ceiling:

- One-off gig work (Fiverr-style, per ad or small batch) — lowest ceiling, fastest to start, good for building a portfolio and testimonials.
- Project-based client work (direct outreach, a batch or campaign per project) — mid ceiling, requires your own outreach but no marketplace fee.
- Retainer/agency work (ongoing monthly batches for a brand) — highest ceiling and most stable, but requires trust built from prior project work.

The natural progression is gig → project → retainer, using each stage's output (finished ads, testimonials) as the pitch for the next stage.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Do It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Set your gig-stage pricing anchored to the documented market range (roughly $10-$55 per ad on freelance marketplaces) — price at the higher end once you have 2-3 portfolio pieces, lower while building initial reviews.
2. Package project-based work as batches (see Module 3), priced $150-$300 per test batch, not per individual ad.
3. Build a portfolio from your best 3-5 ads (real client work if you have it, high-quality practice ads for a real product if not) — this is what actually gets you hired, more than any pitch.
4. Write an outreach message that leads with the finished result (attach or link a sample ad for the prospect's actual product/category) rather than explaining your process.
5. Once you have 2-3 completed projects, pitch a retainer: "ongoing batch production, X ads/month, for $Y/month" — this is where the $1,500-$3,000/month range documented for this work comes in.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Worked Example (AI Video Ads & UGC).

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Worked Example
chunks.text:
Hi [Name] — noticed [Brand] is running paid social ads for [specific product]. I put together a quick AI-generated UGC-style ad using the same product [attach/link the actual sample ad] — thought it might be a useful new angle to test against your current creative. If it's a fit, I can turn around a full batch of variants (different hooks/angles) for testing. Happy to share more examples if useful.

This works because it leads with a finished, product-specific sample — not a pitch about the AI process — and the brand can watch the ad before reading anything else.

Retainer pitch (after 2-3 completed projects):
 "Ongoing batch production: 8 ad variants/month across 2 batches, $2,000/month. Includes scripting, production, 2 revision rounds per batch, and a one-page test-plan write-up per batch tying results back to which hook/angle won."
Priced in the middle of the documented $1,500-$3,000/month range — justified by pointing at the 2-3 prior projects' actual delivered ads, not a generic capability claim.

The progression in numbers: $35/ad gig work (occasional) → $200/batch project work (a few times) → $2,000/month retainer (ongoing) — each stage's finished output becomes the proof that justifies pitching the next stage, rather than restarting the sales pitch from zero each time.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Launch It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Launch It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
This module is business skills, not a production technique — the tool comparison from Modules 1-3 still determines your cost basis: API-based production keeps your cost-per-ad low and predictable for gig/project pricing; local production only changes the math once you're at retainer-level volume where the setup cost amortizes.

How to price it: Anchor to real ranges, don't invent your own from scratch — gig ads $10-$55, project batches $150-$300, retainers $1,500-$3,000/month. Price toward the top of each range once you have proof of quality (portfolio, testimonials), not before.

How to position it: Always lead with the finished ad and the business outcome (more variants to test, faster turnaround, lower cost than a shoot) — never lead with "I use AI to..." Clients are buying results, and over-explaining the AI process invites skepticism about quality instead of building confidence.

Where to find first clients: Freelance marketplaces for your first few gigs and portfolio pieces; direct outreach to DTC brands you can see running paid social ads (visible via each platform's public ad library) for project and retainer-level work — a cold message with a free sample ad for their actual product converts far better than a generic pitch.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Launch It
chunks.text:
The real numbers, and how to talk about them honestly: Named case studies exist of individual brands running AI-UGC-style ad creative at $600K+/month in spend — cite this as evidence the format works at scale, never imply you personally will replicate someone else's ad-spend figure. When you publish your own results, publish the actual number and how it was measured (see the cross-track "Show Your Real Numbers" module) — this is your biggest trust advantage over competitors making vague income claims.

Handling revisions, honestly: landing the sale isn't the end of the work — every price above (gig, batch, retainer) needs a stated number of revision rounds before you quote it, not after a client asks. One free round is standard; scope it as "1 revision round included" in the listing/proposal itself (see the retainer template), and treat anything beyond that as new work, not a favor. Two situations come up often:
- The client wants something the model genuinely can't do well (a very specific product interaction, an exact competitor-ad shot-for-shot copy) — say so directly and offer the closest alternative, rather than burning 3 revision rounds trying to force it. Clients respect a clear "here's what's realistic" more than a vague "let me try."

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Launch It
chunks.text: - Vague feedback ("make it pop more") — turn it into a specific question ("do you mean a faster cut, a different hook, or a different CTA?") before redoing anything. Guessing wrong wastes a revision round on both sides.

2. Medium: Write a cold outreach message to a real DTC brand, including a sample ad you produced for their product category.
3. Hard: Draft a retainer proposal (scope, monthly ad count, price, revision policy) as if pitching a real brand after 2 successful projects.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown (AI Video Ads & UGC).
Learn to reverse-engineer a winning ad instead of guessing what worked.

Track: AI Video Ads & UGC
Time: ~30 minutes
Prerequisites: How AI UGC Actually Works, Pricing & Selling UGC Ads

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / The Problem (AI Video Ads & UGC).
It's easy to produce ads. It's harder to know which elements of a successful ad actually drove its performance, versus which were incidental. Without a teardown method, you end up copying surface style (a trending sound, a specific creator look) without understanding the structural reasons an ad worked — which means you can't reliably reproduce success for a different product.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / The Concept (AI Video Ads & UGC).
A teardown separates an ad into the same five layers from Module 1 — script, avatar/voice, video, captions, export — and asks, for each layer, "what choice was made here, and why might it matter?" This turns "that ad performed well" into a checklist of reusable decisions, rather than a vibe.

Documented, large-scale AI-UGC ad campaigns are useful teardown subjects precisely because their spend level implies the brand tested and kept what worked — the surviving ad reflects real performance data, not a guess.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Do It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Pick a real, currently-running ad in your target product category (visible via a platform's public ad library) that's been running for a while — longevity is a signal it's performing, since brands cut losing ads quickly.
2. Transcribe the script and map it to the hook/pitch/proof/CTA structure from Module 1 — note what makes the hook work specifically (what question/claim/visual, and why it stops a scroll).
3. Note the avatar/voice choice — tone, apparent age/demographic match to the product's audience, energy level.
4. Note the video structure — how much is talking-head vs. b-roll, and where cuts happen relative to the script beats.
5. Note captioning style — timing, emphasis (bold/highlighted keywords), whether it's synced tightly to speech.
6. Write down 2-3 structural takeaways you could apply to a different product — not "copy this ad," but "this kind of hook works for this kind of problem."

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Worked Example (AI Video Ads & UGC).

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Worked Example
chunks.text:
Step 3 — why it likely works: the hook never mentions the product — it's a relatable complaint first, which is why it probably clears a decent hook-rate (viewers watch past 3 seconds to find out what happened) before the pitch even starts. The before/after proof with a day-count is a concrete, checkable claim, not "amazing results."

Step 4 — the takeaway you'd reuse, written generically (not naming the brand): "A pain-first hook that withholds the product name for the first few seconds, paired with a dated before/after, works well for skincare-category ads — the curiosity gap is what earns the watch-through."

Using it in outreach: "I noticed a running ad in the skincare-serum category using a pain-first hook + dated before/after proof — that structure is why it's still running after 47 days. Here's a sample ad using the same structure for [prospect's product]." This is a stronger opener than "I make AI ads" because it demonstrates you understood why something works before pitching anything.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Compare Tools (AI Video Ads & UGC).
Teardown is mostly a manual skill (Do It above), but a video-understanding model can do a first-pass breakdown for you — worth knowing about even though the manual version is what actually builds your judgment.

Real test: ran Module 1's GripMount clip through gemini-video-vision (muapi, $0.004/call — a video-in, text-out model) with the prompt "break this into hook/pitch/proof/CTA, and comment on lip-sync quality and video structure." Actual output:

 Hook: "...her immediate, palpable surprise and excitement are very engaging... 'Okay, I did not expect this...' creates immediate curiosity."
 CTA: Missing. "There is no explicit or implied call to action in this short clip. It ends abruptly... A full ad would typically follow up with 'Shop now'..."
 Lip-sync: "Excellent... flawless and perfectly aligned with the audio."
 Structure: "Talking-head. ...there is no b-roll footage."

That's a genuinely correct read — the clip really is just the hook with no CTA, and it caught that.

Manual vs. AI-assisted, honestly:

| | Manual teardown (Do It above) | AI-assisted (gemini-video-vision) |
|---|---|---|
| What it's good for | Building your own judgment — you have to notice why a hook works, not just that it exists | A fast first pass, or a check against your own read when you're not sure |

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
| Speed | Slower — you're watching and thinking | Seconds, and $0.004/call |
| Where it can mislead | Doesn't apply — it's your own read | Can miss context a human would catch (brand history, category norms, why this audience specifically) — treat it as a draft, not a verdict |

Use it as a learning aid (compare its read to your own to check your instincts) or as a time-saver when you're doing a batch of teardowns and can't manually watch every candidate ad — not as a replacement for actually doing the manual version enough times to build the skill yourself.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Launch It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Launch It (AI Video Ads & UGC).
How to use this in sales: A short teardown of a real running ad in a prospect's category — "here's why this ad from [category, not naming competitors by name] is working, and here's how I'd apply the same structure to your product" — is a stronger pitch opener than a generic capabilities pitch, because it demonstrates judgment, not just production ability.

How to position it: Offer a "structural analysis + sample ad" as a low-cost or free first deliverable for prospects who are on the fence — it's fast to produce once you've practiced this skill, and it sells your judgment, not just your tool access.

A note on naming: When doing teardowns for client-facing material, describe competitor ads by category and structure ("a running ad in the skincare-serum category uses a before/after hook"), not by naming the specific brand or ad — this keeps the analysis about the technique, not competitive intelligence gathering.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Exercises
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Exercises (AI Video Ads & UGC).
1. Easy: Tear down one running ad in a product category you're interested in, using the five-layer structure.
2. Medium: Tear down 3 ads in the same category and identify what's common across all three (a shared structural pattern) versus what's unique to each.
3. Hard: Apply a teardown's structural takeaway to produce a new ad for a different product, and write down which specific choice you borrowed and why.

### 1. How AI UGC Actually Works

 A UGC ad is just five pieces stitched together — once you can see the seams, you can make any of them.

- The 5-stage pipeline: Script → Avatar/Voice → Video → Captions → Export
- Writing a 30-second hook/pitch/proof/CTA script

### 2. Character & Face Consistency

chunks.title: Track 1: AI Video Ads & UGC
chunks.text:
If your AI creator looks like a different person in every shot, nobody will pay for the ad.

- The single most common failure point in AI-generated content

- A drift-check workflow, and when a one-time LoRA training pass pays for itself

Templates: character-consistency-checklist.md

 Clients don't buy one ad — they buy variants to test. Batching is the actual product.

- Delivering a batch with a test plan the client can actually use

 The production is the easy part now. Getting paid for it is a different skill.

- Building a portfolio from your first few pieces
- Outreach that leads with a finished sample, not your process
